sentences: Parisians are spending a Sunday afternoon on La Grande Jatte, an island in the Seine.
The canvas is over two metres high and three metres wide, so standing before it feels like stepping into the park.
Across sun and shade, people pause in stillness.
Georges Seurat painted this in stages between 1884 and 1886.
He spent nearly two years on dozens of studies, calculating the place of every figure.
The finished canvas made its debut at the last Impressionist exhibition, in May 1886.
Start at the riverbank on the upper left.
Sailboats and rowing boats drift on the water, and a woman stands quietly fishing at the edge.
Some read her fishing rod as a sly double meaning, a hint at the island's reputation.
By a tree near the water, a man is playing a horn, and beside him two soldiers in red trousers stand stiffly upright.
People from many different classes share the same park and the same Sunday leisure.
In the centre stand a little girl in white and a woman holding a parasol.
Seurat wrote that he wanted modern people to move like figures on ancient friezes.
So unlike spontaneous Impressionism, the scene is frozen and sculptural.
On the right, a gentleman in a top hat stands beside a woman with a parasol.
The profile of her bustled skirt is as crisp as a paper cut-out silhouette.
They are the largest figures in the whole park.
Look down at her feet.
A monkey on a leash stands there with its tail curled.
Add the little dog bounding beside it and the black dog to the left, and you see how many puzzling details are hidden in this scene.
Now come right up to the grass.
Seurat did not mix colours on the palette; he set small dots of pure colour side by side.
From a distance they blend in the viewer's eye, an effect called optical mixing.
This technique, pointillism, was an experiment grounded in the colour science of his day, drawn from thinkers like Chevreul.
But the zinc yellow Seurat used began darkening to brown even in his lifetime, so today's colours differ slightly from the originals.
Now trace the edge of the canvas.
Around 1888 and 1889, Seurat repainted a border of blue, orange and red dots, enclosing the picture in its own frame.
The Art Institute of Chicago has even recreated the white frame he designed for it.
Step back and take in the whole scene again.
The Art Institute of Chicago bought the painting in 1924, and it still hangs there today.
Move between dots up close and people from afar, and find the distance where the colours start to blend.
